title: Clean Architecture in .NET
description: Build maintainable .NET applications following Clean Architecture principles with dependency inversion, separation of concerns, and onion/hexagonal architecture patterns.

data.text: Clean Architecture: The Dependency Inversion Principle

Clean Architecture, as described by Robert C. Martin, inverts the traditional dependency flow. Instead of high-level modules depending on low-level implementation details, both depend on abstractions. The direction of dependencies always points inward toward the core domain — infrastructure and frameworks depend on the domain, never the other way around.

data.caption: Clean Architecture concentric layers with inward-pointing dependencies

        Entities["Domain Entities\n(Aggregates, Value Objects)"]
        Interfaces["Domain Interfaces\n(IRepository, IEmailService)"]

    end

        Email["Email/SMS Providers\nExternal API Clients"]
        Auth["Authentication\n(Entra ID, JWT)"]
    end

rows: No external dependencies — only primitives and built-in types
Implements domain interfaces; depends on EF Core, SDKs, Auth libraries
Controllers reference Application DTOs and services

data.text: Dependency Injection at the Composition Root

The composition root is where the dependency graph is assembled. In ASP.NET Core, this happens in Program.cs / Startup. All domain interfaces are bound to concrete implementations here, keeping the domain layer ignorant of infrastructure details.

data.text: Onion vs Hexagonal vs Clean Architecture

These terms are often used interchangeably but have nuances. Onion Architecture (Fowler) emphasizes domain at the center. Hexagonal Architecture (CQRS) emphasizes ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations). Clean Architecture unifies these into concentric layers with dependency rule arrows.

data.title: Common Anti-Patterns to Avoid
data.text: 1. The 'Big Ball of Mud' — no layer boundaries. 2. Domain projects referencing Infrastructure directly. 3. Controllers containing business logic. 4. Cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth) scattered across domain code. 5. Leaky abstractions where EF entities are used as DTOs.

data.title: Refactoring Exercise: Layer Boundary Violation
data.description: Given a codebase where the Presentation layer directly queries a DbContext, refactor to introduce a repository interface in the Domain layer and an Infrastructure implementation.
steps: Identify all direct DbContext usage in controllers
Define an IRepository interface in the Domain layer
Create an EF Core implementation in the Infrastructure layer
Register the implementation at the composition root
data.expectedOutcome: Controllers depend only on IRepository, not on EF Core. Domain layer has no references to any infrastructure.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Dependencies always point inward — frameworks depend on domain, not vice versa
Domain layer contains no external dependencies — pure business logic
DI composition root binds abstractions to implementations at startup
Layer isolation prevents tight coupling and enables independent testing
Common variants: Onion, Hexagonal, and Clean Architecture share core principles
data.takeaway: Clean Architecture creates a foundation where domain logic remains stable while infrastructure and presentation evolve independently.
